Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Monday, 15 April 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 016)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney with Mr Hilbert Chiu for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning. Mr Muston?
MR MUSTON: Do you need to receive appearances from
everyone who is here?
THE COMMISSIONER: No, I don't think so. We've already
done that.
MR MUSTON: Commissioner, opening the inquiry late last
year we spoke of the resilience of the New South Wales
health system and the high standard of care that it is able
to deliver under what are often very challenging
circumstances. We think it is worth pausing to note that
that is something which it has again demonstrated in spades
in its response to the tragic events in Bondi over the
weekend.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR MUSTON: We're embarking upon a hearing block which has
as its focus terms of reference B and D. In practical
terms, we will be examining the governance and
decision-making structures within the public health system
and exploring the way in which they impact on the system's
ability to identify and meet the health needs of the
population it serves.
Like the earlier hearing blocks, these areas of focus
will obviously have significant interaction and overlap
with other terms of reference. It is impossible, really,
to confine the evidence or the hearing, the hearing block
that we have, strictly to one term of reference or another
but, in any event, it is our idea that we will try, as best
as we can, to confine this hearing block to those issues.
Obviously, this won't be the last time we see these
issues either. We're going to have to look at
decision-making and governance structures, for example, in
future regional hearings as we look at the way in which
health is delivered by the health system in those areas.
Nevertheless, those are the issues that we're focusing on
principally for the next two weeks.
Governance can probably be divided into two broad
areas, corporate governance and clinical governance. It
also operates differently at different levels within each
of the various components of the health system and at its

heart, it is all about decision-making and direction.
Our particular focus over the next two weeks will be
examining how that decision-making operates at those
different levels, so within the ministry, within the pillar
organisations, within LHDs, and within affiliated health
organisations.
You will have seen, hopefully, the witness list that
we have set out for this hearing block.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR MUSTON: There is a lot of evidence to get through in a
relatively limited period of time, unless there is any
particular questions at this stage that we can assist you
with, Commissioner, we will move immediately to our first
witness, who is Fiona Wilkinson, the director of clinical
governance at the Central Coast LHD.
THE COMMISSIONER: Go ahead, thank you.
MR MUSTON: Dr Waterhouse will take that witness.
DR WATERHOUSE: I call Fiona Wilkinson.
<FIONA WILKINSON, affirmed: [10.04am]
<EXAMINATION BY DR WATERHOUSE:
DR WATERHOUSE: Q. Can you please state your full name
and your position?
A. My name is Fiona Wilkinson and I am the district
director of quality, strategy and improvement at Central
Coast Local Health District.
Q. Can you briefly outline your qualifications and
experience that have led to this role?
A. Yes. So my background, I was initially a registered
nurse and worked for many years in an emergency department.
I then have moved into improvement science and I have
a masters degree in MBT - masters of business and
technology.
Q. You have, as I understand it, quite a large and
diverse portfolio, and under that you manage a number of
teams?

A. Correct.
Q. I would like to start with the clinical governance
team that is under you. Now, clinical governance in the
Central Coast Local Health District, as I understand it,
also includes oversight of volunteers, consumers, and
libraries?
A. That's correct.
Q. Can you explain the connection between those, how it
has come to be formed like that?
A. Yes. They all interrelate with delivering safe
quality care. The input of consumers in advising an
organisation in design and input into care delivery, and
volunteers play a very important role in assisting our
clinical teams in supporting to deliver care.
Libraries - libraries add a research value, an
evidence-based value and also tie in for that reason.
Q. Now, I understand that there is a separate director of
safety, quality and governance; is that the correct title?
A. That's correct.
Q. And does that person report to you?
A. Correct.
Q. Is there any other person to whom they report?
A. They also have a dual line of reporting for the chief
executive and that line is for serious adverse events,
serious complaints, major clinical governance issues.
Q. So is it correct to say that for the bulk of their
role day to day, they report to you and there are just
particular aspects to which they report to the chief
executive?
A. Correct.
Q. How does that work, operationally, from your point of
view - the dual reporting, that is?
A. Operationally, we work at Central Coast with an
accountability matrix and a delegation matrix, and that
works efficiently following that matrix. Operationally,
that director reports to me on a daily basis. We manage
our work flows with huddles, so we will have a huddle twice
a week and also monthly accountability meetings that that
director and I discuss key accountabilities and activities

in her work role.
Q. So you find it is an effective way to manage it.
A. It is effective.
Q. How would you define "clinical governance"?
A. Clinical governance is delivering safe, high quality,
effective care.
Q. And what are your personal responsibilities for
clinical governance?
A. So I'm accountable for ensuring that systems and
processes are in place to deliver safe, high quality,
effective care.
Q. And how does that compare with the director that
reports to you?
A. The director that reports to me is actually running
those systems and processes, so ensuring that they are in
place, actively participating at varying levels. That
director has a team underneath that role of patient safety
and quality roles, as well as what we term "consumer
feedback" roles, which manage complaints and concerns
directly with customers.
Q. How many people would be reporting in that team to the
director?
A. A total of I think it's 38 FTE.
Q. 38 FTE. And that's across the district?
A. Across the district, correct.
Q. Are they all based in the same unit or are they
dispersed across different sites?
A. They are dispersed across. So we have two main sites,
so they are primarily dispersed across those two sites, but
their work takes them across all areas and they are
representative in key safety and quality meetings on those
sites.
Q. Does the director of clinical safety, quality and
governance travel around the district to different sites
overseeing those systems?
A. Correct. So that director sits primarily at Gosford
Hospital, our tertiary site, but also sits at Wyong
Hospital one day a week.

Q. And you yourself, do you travel because of the
clinical governance responsibilities you have?
A. Because of all of my responsibilities, it takes me to
all of the sites.
Q. And when you visit those sites, are you looking at
clinical governance?
A. I think when you have worked in the area of safety and
quality for a long time, you always have a safety and
quality hat on and strive to improve, so whilst I might be
there for specific purposes, you always are wearing that
hat and looking at safety and quality.
Q. Given the range of responsibilities that you have, how
do you ensure that the right systems are in place at the
right places for the needs of different services?
A. So there is various checks and balances that assist in
identifying if those systems are in place. One of those is
the accreditation system, so that's one tool in the tool
kit. We have audits of which the sites are responsible,
for managing audits, we have a series of indicators that we
monitor and manage for each of those sites. Whilst on
those sites, we, both the leaders on the sites, the
executive and also the board, conduct safety rounds which
provides an opportunity to check directly in with staff and
teams, and we have a series of governance meetings which
cascade from an executive level down to a team level.
Q. I might go through some of those in a little bit more
detail, if that's okay. First of all, can you just briefly
tell us about the accreditation process that's in place?
A. Okay. So all organisations are required to be
accredited. Accreditation occurs every three to five years
and we're accredited against the national safety and
quality standards, of which there are eight standards. Our
accreditation is actually due this year. Accreditation is
run on a short notice survey, so we will receive notice on
a Thursday that the surveyors will be on site the following
week and will attend our sites the following week and
actually review our accreditation processes.
In our previous accreditation we were commended on the
strength of our clinical governance processes, and that was
in 2021.
Q. And you mentioned that there are audits done. Can you
describe what those are?

A. Yes. So we have routine audits through what we call
a CEWA system, which is run by the Clinical Excellence
Commission, and they are routine against the national
standards and any other areas that have been defined for
audit, and they are conducted by our clinicians and our
clinical teams.
Q. Now, you mentioned indicators. Can you just describe
what those are?
A. So key performance indicators. So we have --
Q. I might come back to those. I just wanted to check
that's what you meant by those. I will come back to those
in a moment. Safety rounds, what do they involve?
A. Safety rounds involve a leader, so a leader from the
clinical services or from the site. So you might have
a director of nursing and an operational nurse manager
walking around and talking to staff, asking them what's
working well, opportunities to improve, any challenges. We
undertake the same process with our executive, so we have
a rotating roster for an individual executive and a board
member to conduct what we title our executive walk-arounds,
and undertake that same process and seek feedback from the
clinical teams.
Q. Can you think of any examples where that has led to
a system improvement?
A. Yes, I can. In doing that, you are able to identify
if there are any consistent themes, so whilst they are
rotated, and there is an example on one of the sites where
there was difficulty in accessing bariatric beds, so
a specific type of equipment to manage larger patients, and
that theme was coming up consistently across that site, so
there was then a process review as a result of that and an
ordering - a review of the procurement process around those
beds, the number we had on site and the accessibility, the
ability to be able to locate those beds when needed, and
a process change as a result.
Q. Now, you mentioned the Clinical Excellence Commission
briefly.
A. Yes.
Q. I will just refer to that for simplicity as the CEC,
which it is to be known as.
A. Thank you.

Q. Is the CEC involved in leading or supporting clinical
governance within the LHD?
A. Yes.
Q. Can you explain how it plays that role? What does it
do?
A. Okay. So there is a couple of mechanisms. Capability
is one, where we work very closely with the CEC on the
implementation of safety and quality capability improvement
programs. We have those embedded within the organisation,
tying in with our improvement programs, and that plays
a very important role in that.
Q. What do you mean by "capability" there?
A. Building staff knowledge in safety and quality and
awareness.
Q. And do you find that the initiatives brought in by the
CEC or required by the CEC - do they come with additional
resources to be able to embed them in the LHD?
A. The CEC does support those initiatives with a small
amount of funds for us to be able to apply, which we apply
centrally to one of my other teams, the improvement team,
and combine that with our other improvement programs.
Q. Is that enough to be able to implement and embed those
things?
A. I think there's always opportunity to enhance those
resources.
Q. If you go on, you were going to say there is another
role the CEC plays?
A. The CEC provides a key role in sharing learnings
across the state, so any serious adverse events are
reviewed by the CEC and learnings are fed back to
organisations; a key role in any recalls in products and
notification and management of that; guidance, education to
our safety and quality program; a key support for the role
that reports directly to me.
Q. You mentioned recalls. Can you just explain for the
Inquiry what that might involve?
A. If there is a product recall that needs to be removed
from circulation that could place a risk to harm, the CEC
manages that notification, of which we then act upon in the
district.

Q. How often would that happen in health?
A. Every couple of weeks.
Q. So it would have to be - everything would have to be
removed. Say it was a product on the ward or in theatres,
they would just have to pull those all off the shelf,
effectively?
A. The LHDs need to enact - it would - it happens more
frequently, but with smaller consequences. Ones that have
a major impact could be every couple of weeks. So you
might be removing an item off the shelf, it might be, for
example, an ampoule of normal saline of a certain batch
number, that we then put a process in place to remove those
items from circulation.
Q. How resource intensive is that process?
A. It is resource intensive. It involves a wide range of
staff from pharmacy to nursing unit managers, to staff on
the floor.
Q. Does it ever result in delays, if you have to remove
all of something that was being used for patient care and
have to get a new replacement in?
A. There is normally a substitute item.
Q. Now, you mentioned governing committees before and
I understand that you are the executive sponsor of the
health care quality committee; is that correct?
A. Correct.
Q. Can you just explain what is meant by the term
"executive sponsor", what that involves you having to do?
A. Okay. I coordinate items to come to the committee;
coordinate evidence. That committee makes a selection
annually on the priorities that that committee is going to
focus on, so coordinating any literature or evidence to
allow decisions to be informed.
Q. Who chairs the committee?
A. The committee is chaired by a board member.
Q. And does this mean that you, in your role as executive
sponsor, effectively guide the work of the committee and
decide what they will review?
A. In partnership with the executive sponsor.
Q. Sorry --

A. Sorry, with the chair, apologies. Thank you.
Q. Who are the members of the health care quality
committee?
A. We have three board members on that committee and
members of the executive.
Q. And are there any other external people such as
consumers?
A. There is one consumer and also the director of
clinical safety, quality and governance.
Q. Any GPs or other --
A. No, not on that one.
Q. Are there clinicians that are active in the hospitals
that you --
A. No, we have the district director of medical services
as one of our executive.
Q. So with that sort of make-up, are there people with
particular expertise, either from the board or the
executive, apart from yourself, in clinical governance?
A. Yes, there is.
Q. And who would they be?
A. So the director that reports to me is on there; the
board chair - the committee chair; the district director of
nursing; and then the other two representatives are from
the operations teams and the chief executive as well.
Q. Do you find that there ever develops a disconnect, if
there are no clinicians on that committee, with trying to
sort of communicate with them about what is important to
them?
A. The connection actually comes from the committee that
sits below that committee, which has clinicians,
operational managers, general managers on it, which is
quite a large subcommittee and really collates other
subcommittees, reviews items before they come up to health
care quality committee. So there is a process of
systematic review before it gets - and feedback into items,
before they actually get to health care quality committee.
Q. So what's that subordinate committee called?
A. It is clinical safety, quality and governance
committee.

Q. So the clinical safety, quality and governance
committee reports to the health care quality committee?
A. Correct.
Q. And then what does the health care quality committee
report to?
A. The board, directly to the board.
Q. How often does the health care quality committee meet?
A. Monthly.
Q. And what about the --
A. The subcommittee.
Q. I'm getting mixed up with the names. The
subcommittee.
A. The subcommittee also meets monthly.
Q. And is that coordinated in such a way that concerns
being raised by the clinicians will be fed through to the
HCQC, if I can abbreviate it to that --
A. Yes, that's exactly right.
Q. -- in a timely manner?
A. Exactly. So the committees are offset in their timing
in the month to allow something to be tabled at the
subcommittee, reviewed, input, and then to be tabled at the
next level, if it is required - if a decision is required
to be made at a sub-board committee level, it is then
tabled at HCQC.
Q. And what about sort of communication in the opposite
direction, so either from the board or from the HCQC down
through to that subcommittee and, more broadly, to
clinicians?
A. Yes, so that mechanism happens in two ways, and that's
shared membership on each committee, but also, importantly,
in all of our committees we - at the end of the meeting the
last item in the agenda is key messages, and so we actually
record, usually three, key messages and those key messages
are from that meeting and those messages flow both up and
flow down back to the subcommittee or up to the board and
outline key important matters that occurred in that
meeting.
Q. And when you say they flow back up and back down, how

does a physiotherapist in a community health service come
to know about those key messages?
A. Okay. That would go through that role, the director
of those services, so it would flow back. Sitting on the
subcommittee is the director of allied health and so any
important messages would go back through that director of
allied health.
Q. Are the minutes from the HCQC meetings and the
subcommittee meetings available on the website?
A. On the intranet, the intranet.
Q. Can you outline for me what the purpose of the HCQC is
from your perspective?
A. The HCQC is the peak governing body for safety and
quality, so they have several functions. So they are
accountable for signing off the attestation statement that
the LHD is meeting the requirements of accreditation and
safety and quality, which goes to the board; they have
responsibility --
Q. Sorry, I am just going to stop you there. It goes to
the board. Does it go anywhere else, that attestation
statement?
A. No, final sign-off is by the board.
Q. Is there any feedback of the information on that
attestation to the ministry or the CEC or --
A. Yes, it goes to the - from the board to the CEC and
the ministry. That's a requirement of LHDs.
Q. Sorry, please go on. You were saying about the
functions of the committee.
A. That committee reviews key performance indicators and
looks at the level of performance at an LHD level. It
identifies key safety and quality priorities and sets those
for the district, and ensures that all of those safety and
quality systems and processes are in place.
Q. And how as a committee does it ensure those systems
are in place?
A. By reviewing the information that comes to the
committee that provides evidence of that. So the papers,
essentially.
Q. How does it determine the priorities - annual
priorities?

A. So the starting point is usually the KPIs. The
committee below provides recommendations on priorities, so
through a combination of things, looking at the KPIs,
feedback from the subcommittees, feedback from clinical
council. We engage with clinical council to seek
information as well. We align to ensure alignment of those
priorities to the district strategic plan, and any evidence
and literature support.
Q. You just mentioned clinical council. Can you explain
where that fits into the mix of committees that we've been
talking about?
A. The clinical council occurs monthly and is
a requirement of the Health Services Act and has a variety
of clinicians on that council and it provides a very useful
environment to take anything that you would like to feed
back, to have that discussion in clinical council.
Q. So would there be some opportunity for a combination
of some of those things? I'm just wondering why you need -
the clinical council is maybe a requirement, but why do you
need two other committees in addition to that? Would it be
possible to combine some of those functions?
A. I would think not. All of those functions have quite
large agendas and I think our committee structure has been
tabled, I think time wise, you wouldn't - it wouldn't be an
effective way to run a meeting.
Q. And when you say they have large agendas, what
proportion of those agendas would be noting things that are
happening as opposed to making active decisions that will
result in changes?
A. Maybe 50 per cent.
Q. So 50 per cent they are noting things, progress with
things or events that have occurred, and 50 per cent they
are making decisions that will lead to changes for patient
safety and quality?
A. Correct.
Q. I'd like to talk a bit more about the KPIs, if I may.
So what is the role of the HCQC, first, in relation to
KPIs?
A. Provides oversight, and so the KPIs indicate
performance against key criteria, and so the HCQC monitors
that performance and looks at the performance levels across
those various indicators.

Q. And are they looking at it by facility, by service, by
clinical unit? How does it work?
A. So, at that level, we report at a district level, but
each indicator is broken down on that report by facility.
So if something is not performing, you can then see which
facility is not performing against that particular KPI.
Q. What happens if a unit or a facility is not performing
or that there is perhaps a worrying trend, if I can put it
that way? What does the HCQC do?
A. So the HCQC would initially monitor, but then the way
we report, we provide a brief analysis of what is
occurring, so if there are any special calls or
circumstances, so there may be a known event that has
pushed that KPI outside its parameters, so that would be
noted and reported in the report. If there is continuing
non-performance or you were seeing a trend, a decline in
performance, the various executive would then engage and
work with their teams, so the general managers or the
directors of nursing, to look at opportunities for
improvement. That would then be reported in that report as
well, what those improvement activities are.
Q. So the - they would monitor it, they would - changes
would occur. Would there be any feedback to continue
looking at whether those changes have been effective?
A. And that occurs through the subcommittee. So those -
the person that is accountable for delivering those changes
will report through the subcommittee. That is then
recorded in that report that comes to that - to the HCQC.
So it is continually monitored.
Q. Can you give me an example of where that's happened -
like where there has been an adverse trend, say, and works
that needed to be done?
A. I could give you multiple examples. I will draw on
one, which would be unplanned readmissions within 28 days.
So probably close to 18 months ago we were seeing a trend
of increasing unplanned readmissions. An improvement
program was put in place as a result of that. That trend
was on both sites, the two acute sites, and we saw
a significant improvement. A large piece of diagnostic
work was undertaken to see what the cause was. And then,
recently - and there was considerable improvement and it
was monitoring as performing, but recently, we have seen an
upward trend again in the unplanned readmissions, so the

executive accountable for that area on health care quality
committee have put further actions in place to again review
the cause and put improvement processes in place.
Q. In determining what actions are required, what the
causes are, is there - who do they consult with?
A. So they consult with their teams, so that's - because
that's the facilities, that's commencing with the general
managers on the site and then working directly with
clinicians, drilling down on data and information to see,
looking at cohorts of patients and then working with those
clinical teams to look for opportunities to improve.
Q. Now, I understand that the HCQC has also given some
direction in relation to hospital-acquired complications.
Can you outline a bit of the work that's been involved with
that?
A. Correct. So we were seeing a trend of non-performing
hospital-acquired complications and initiated a large
improvement program, of which we stood up dedicated
governance around that to guide that improvement program,
and --
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. What is a non-performing
hospital-acquired complication?
A. The complications, each have indicators. There are 14
hospital-acquired complications and so their level of
performance was outside the tolerance band.
Q. I see.
A. So they were not performing within the tolerance band
for our LHD within our service agreement.
Q. And for the unplanned readmissions within 28 days, you
said a large piece of diagnostic work was undertaken to see
what the cause was. What is the detail of a large piece of
diagnostic work - what does that mean?
A. So that commences with reviewing our data to
understand the cohorts of the patients that are actually
returning to the organisation. So starting with the data
and then actually interviewing staff and understanding
processes, and it's often a step-by-step process review.
Q. And was there a sole cause found for the unplanned
readmissions, or was it more complex than that?
A. It is complex and multiple causes.

Q. With multiple causes, then, how was it improved?
A. Really taking each problem at a time and putting an
improvement process around that. So an example would be
discharge summaries. So there is evidence that if
a patient on discharge visits a GP within seven days, then
there are reduced unplanned --
Q. Chances of coming back to hospital?
A. Are minimised.
Q. Sorry, did that involve - sorry, you continue.
A. So that involved ensuring that there is timely
discharge summaries, that our patient had a copy of the
discharge summaries, and that our GPs are receiving
discharge summaries.
Q. So an improvement in at least the timeliness of
discharge summaries saw an improvement in unplanned
readmissions within 28 days?
A. Correct. Correct. And then another example is
a process change. So there are some patients that we
actually ask to come back, and if that's not recorded as
being requested to return to the hospital for a review - it
might be a wound, it might be an injury, a fracture - then,
on return, it's then recorded as an unplanned readmission,
so the result of that is a process change, an
administrative process change.
Q. And with the discharge summaries and - I assume one is
an issue of timeliness, two is an issue of I suppose the
adequacy of the discharge summary?
A. Correct.
Q. How accurate it is and that the information in it is
the most pertinent for the patient's condition?
A. Correct.
Q. What steps, if you recall, were put in place to make
sure that there was an improvement in both of those things
in relation to discharge summaries?
A. The greatest step is timeliness and ensuring access by
the GPs and, unfortunately, our systems don't always
connect.
Q. Just explain what you mean by that.
A. So the discharge summary automatically goes into My
Health Record but the GPs may not always access My Health

Record. So providing a patient a copy to actually have in
their hand was an important step.
Q. And that was a reform, if you like, was it?
A. Correct.
Q. And who, in the main, creates the discharge summaries?
Is it the junior doctors, is it the treating clinician?
Who is it?
A. The junior doctors.
Q. And were there any steps taken in relation to the
junior doctors to ensure that the discharge summaries had
the most pertinent information and were timely as well?
A. There is. Clinical documentation in most of these
improvement programs is a very important matter,
particularly in hospital-acquired complications, and so
working with the JMO teams to improve documentation.
Q. And when you say "working with the JMO teams", what
does that involve? Does that involve the more senior
clinicians providing some better training, if you like,
or - you tell me?
A. Yes, as leaders, so the SMOs, the senior medical
officers and the senior registrars, as leaders, coaching
the junior medical officers. But the - they don't sit
within my teams but in the medical services, they have
training, education programs.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
DR WATERHOUSE: Q. Just one further question in relation
to the unplanned readmission. You said that there had been
a significant improvement but then it started to --
A. Decline.
Q. -- go outside the trend again. When you went back and
looked, when the team did, did they find that that was
because some of the steps that had been taken had not been
embedded effectively, perhaps there had been a changeover
in junior doctors or whatever, or were there new issues
that were identified?
A. They are still working through that, but what my
knowledge is, they are finding some very complex patients
with multiple comorbidities returning, and they are
focusing with the community teams how they can better
manage those patients.

Q. So it's more about a subset of patients that need
additional attention --
A. Correct.
Q. Than a general deterioration in that program?
A. Correct.
Q. Just with the hospital-acquired complications, can you
give us examples of a few of those? I understand you said
there are 14, but just to give us an idea of the sorts of
things we're talking about.
A. The type of complications?
Q. Yes.
A. Falls is a complication; health care associated
infections, which has multiple subsets underneath it;
pressure injuries is a complication. There are respiratory
complications, medication complications, birth trauma.
Q. What is the relationship between those examples that
you give and the accreditation system? Does it look at
those particular types of complications?
A. The accreditation system will view those as well.
Q. Can you go into any more detail about how that occurs?
A. Those complications will relate to the various
standards, into the eight standards, and they will be

prevent leading to complications.

the service agreement?

A. Correct.

between local health districts or facilities, perhaps, but

A. Correct.

A. Not directly.

KPI based on the feedback?

but I just can't think of an example at this point.

Health District?

rates.

facilities and community health services, et cetera?

dashboards, but as you can imagine, if you are a nursing
unit manager on a ward, and you are looking at a rate at an
LHD level, it has very little meaning. We have improvement
programs throughout the district where the wards can set
their own KPIs. The facilities have a KPI and then - that
all feed up to delivering that KPI in the service
agreement. So the NUM on the ward might simply be
recording the number of, for example, falls that have
occurred on that ward, rather than looking at the total
rate as a district.
Q. In the years that you have been in this role, or
clinical governance roles more broadly, how much change has

there been in the KPIs?

There's been some variation in the HACs, some variation in
the access indicators. The access indicators are under
review at the moment, bringing learnings in what adds
value, so there will be continued change in those. So
there is always a small percentage of change that occurs
annually through learnings.

they tend to be consistent year to year, is that what I'm
hearing?
A. Fairly consistent.
Q. Have they tended to grow in number significantly over
the years? Do they keep adding to them, or do they take
some away that are no longer apparently relevant?
A. It is probably on balance, if something comes off,
it's replaced with something else. I would not say that
they grow.
Q. I wouldn't say, sorry?
A. I wouldn't say they grow.
Q. So they maintain a relatively stable number?
A. Mmm.
Q. From your perspective, with your experience, how
effective would you say that the KPIs in the service
agreement are for measuring safety and quality of patient
care?

A. Yes.
Q. Would you make any changes to them if you had more
involvement in setting the KPIs?

improved in your local health district?

management process, and that is being undertaken by the CEC
now, with engagement with key staff and the design of that
policy. That policy had significant improvements in 2020
and improvements in the way we constitute a team to design
recommendations, and that has been a considerable benefit.

policy to ensure that investigations add value.
Q. That would be a statewide change, would it, or is that

specific to your district?
A. That will be a statewide change.

management policy currently in place present for your
district which is leading to your involvement in that
change?

improved further.

make in the coming year or so in terms of clinical

improve that learning, embed training in safety and
quality, and ensuring that staff are comfortable and safe,
that level of psychological safety, to raise issues. We

committees, allowing them to be broadened to
multidisciplinary teams, and a safe and secure environment

undertake an external audit and work with us on improvement

eyes. There is a process around monitoring hand hygiene,

that level of independence.

A. It would probably be an opportunity.

that you have a health care improvement team. What is that
team responsible for?

projects, improvement projects; a responsibility for
building capability in the organisation, so they run
several improvement programs. The team is also responsible
for health planning, so we have two health planners in that
team, which is - the accountability there is for the
delivery of the strategic plan, the clinical services plan,
any key planning documents.

within the district?
A. Yes, they do.

A. So that's working with the various general managers
and clinicians to implement individual projects using
a methodology. We use Lean Six Sigma, which is looking
at - exactly looking at efficiency and defects and working
with clinicians on the floor to implement those improvement
projects.
Q. Can you give us an example of where that has been
implemented using Lean Six Sigma?
A. Yes, there is multiple improvement projects with Lean
Six Sigma. As part of the training, the attendees'
requirement is to run an improvement project. So there are
several per year. On a large scale, access improvement has
been the biggest areas where they have run those projects.
So looking at length of stay in the inpatient units,
running a project to reduce length of stay, to identify
barriers to discharge, and planning.

Q. And so that has been done in multiple different
services within the district?
A. Correct.
Q. Are you able to explain the sort of degree of
reduction that there has been in terms of length of stay?
A. If you - if I take our KPIs as an example, length of
stay, there has been a reduction, I can't think what we are
now, around 3.6 days, but there has been significant
reductions in specialty areas. But overall, our KPIs for
access performance have improved significantly over the
last two years, with focus and improvement programs.

waits in ED and --
A. Correct. Transfer of care, so time off the ambulance
stretcher, waits in ED, length of time in ED.
Q. Does the team undertake initiatives to identify and
reduce waste?
A. So it's around efficiency and effectiveness, which
absolutely is waste, and even if you take the HACs as an
example - hospital complications - there is waste if
we're - if there are areas where patients are ending up
with a complication. So most of our programs are removing
waste.
Q. So that might be waste of time, effectively?
A. Yes.
Q. What about waste of resources?
A. That includes waste of resources.

the changes that the team identifies?
A. I think in improvement there are always challenges
embedding things. You've got a constant turnover of staff
with your junior medical workforce, a constant turnover, so
it is often that you're going back, you are reinforcing
that change, you are putting systems and processes in for
relevant managers to reinforce that change.

primary health network. Can you outline what that
involves?

an alliance between the LHD and the PHN. We have a charter

where we agree on priorities that we can align those
priorities and work together to deliver outcomes to
improve, really, the health care on the Central Coast.
Q. So those priorities translate to projects?
A. They do.
Q. What sorts of projects do you get involved with with
the PHN?
A. An example, we've run a diabetes project, where at the
moment we're running a chronic pain project. There are
various projects sitting within the mental health teams.

committee. We look at projects in the GP panel as well,
all of which align to the LHD's priorities but also the
PHN's priorities.

project look like in terms of who would be involved, what
would they be doing?

LHD, the PHN teams, but also the general practitioners on
the coast, and so that project was using a support
mechanism for GPs with the expertise of the specialist
staff in the LHD.
Q. And you mentioned a GP panel. Is that a way of
consulting with GPs?

meet every six weeks and we work to have a consulting
process so that if the LHD is implementing a change in your
model of care, a new process, we actually use that
consultative panel work with them to provide feedback into
the design.
Q. How are those seven GPs identified?
A. It's an expression of interest that is run by the PHN,
and they apply for that role.
Q. And are there ways to engage with other GPs beyond
those seven?
A. Yeah. So through the PHN and the LHD we run several
connecting sessions, education sessions, for the broader GP
network.
Q. What arrangements are there in place for consumer
consultation?

often use survey, as an example, to get to the community of
the coast. An example of that is we're undertaking master
planning at the moment on the Wyong Hospital site and

responses in that. Or we will use expressions of interest
out to dedicated groups to provide feedback into design,
design of facilities, design of a model; or we have
consumers as a member of key committees.
Q. Now, say you are developing a new model of care for
diabetes or maybe chronic pain.
A. Mmm-hmm.

develop that?

identify the various stakeholders in that model of care,
and that will often be broader than the LHD. It might be
NSW Ambulance; it would definitely be somebody in PHN; it
might require a GP representative; we would most likely
want a consumer representative and the various
representatives within the LHD.

giving input. What happens next?
A. You would probably be writing a business case to
actually get - establish the costs, the outcomes, the
benefits that are expected in that model of care. That
would go through an approval process, determined where the
funding mechanism comes from, and then, once approved, that
would then move into an implementation model.
Q. Would it be piloted somewhere first generally or --
A. It possibly would. It's difficult when you pilot
things if you need to recruit. So it depends if you are
changing the way existing people are working or you are
commencing something new.

structures, and so it has a series of committees from
engaging with clinicians in design, up through project
control groups, and the final committee, being the
executive steering committee, where you have oversight of
the entire project.

A. Yes, it is.

a capital work, how do you ensure that there is accurate
forecasting of what it is going to cost to run that

fall under the responsibility of health infrastructure.

health infrastructure, complete a financial impact
statement, and the FIS determines the - it projects the

A. No.

be there. It's the LHD and the ministry committing to
those requirements, which can be some years before that
building has opened.

being delivered.

duplication?
A. No, they have different roles.

Shore for approval.

A. Yes, correct.

reviews to see the level of risk and what process that will

to follow.

that pathway?
A. Correct.

line manager. So if you needed somebody released to
undertake the project, released from delivering care to

Q. What is within the concept of "unwarranted clinical
variation" in this concept?
A. Unwarranted clinical variation?
Q. Yes.
A. So it is a broad term, but essentially it relates to
where clinical care varies from an expected norm or an
expected average, and that that variation isn't justified
by the particular individual characteristics of the patient
or the patient cohort. That's sort of a - my
interpretation of that.
Q. How is it monitored?
A. It is - if you appreciate that fairly general
definition, it is not something that's simply monitored by
one set of, for example, performance indicators. Because

it is so broad, it can manifest in a variety of ways, but
I can give you some examples where we have - where the
system aims to provide clarity around an expected norm and
then we can monitor around that. So we have at a statewide
level a program called leading better value care. I'm not
sure whether that's been brought up before now.
Q. Just describe it for us?
A. So it is overarchingly governed by the ACI, the Agency
for Clinical Innovation, another one of the pillars. It is
particular care - models of care that have been
demonstrated at least in one place to have good value and
good outcomes for patients, and has described - that model
of care has been well described and that is then deployed
across the system and implemented across the system at
the local level.
There are probably about 14 or so that are quite
visible to - at the system level at this stage, and we have
implemented most of those models within our health service,
and it allows us, because they've got particular explicit
features that we can identify to see that they are in place
and then are able to monitor how well that is being
performed in terms of the number of patients that are
receiving that particular type of care.
Q. And those models of care become the expected norm that
you referred to in your earlier answer, do they?
A. That's right.

A. Well, usually it is attendant - the model of care is
attendant to a particular specialty, maybe orthopaedic
surgery, for example, so the people delivering the care
themselves will monitor it in an operational sense, then
usually at a facility level, sometimes at the district
level, we'll also look at data to indicate how well that
has been deployed - you know, the number of patients, for
example, who are getting that particular prescribed model
of care. So the governance and oversight of it is where
the care has been delivered, but then also more broadly at
the facility level and then overarchingly at the district
level.
Q. So where the instances of unwarranted clinical
variation are identified, what steps are taken in response?
A. Again, it is hard to be general about that. It is

particularly - it is specific to the particular type of
clinical variation that we're talking about. With those
models of care that I have just mentioned, they are quite
visible, quite measurable, and that can have a more
systematic response.
If you are talking about, say, unwarranted clinical
variation at, say - within a surgical team or teams, where,
say, one doctor takes longer - one surgeon takes longer
than another doctor, for example, could be considered
unwarranted clinical variation, but how you respond to that
is far more difficult and usually that would be about
engaging with the team themselves, providing them with the
data and they work through how - what might be driving that
variation.

variation when, in fact, there may be reasonable
justification for that variation.

the woods, probably slightly different.

A. Well, you could have low value care delivered very
efficiently and effectively and with little variation to
a particular standard. So it's not - there is no
unwarranted variation within the care delivery, but that
doesn't mean necessarily that the care is high value,
because it may still not make much difference to the health
of the individual, for example.

care could be delivered entirely in accordance with an
efficient model of care for that particular instance but it

probably the thing that that's referring to is the health
outcome for the individual.
Q. Yes.

little variation, but in terms of individual health
outcomes and possibly more broadly health outcomes for the

community, it may have little impact.

clinical decision-making and individual clinician

clarity around, because there are so many variables, not
the least of which are patient variation, that may - you
can't just say one particular procedure is low value,
because it may be extremely high value for an individual;
maybe across the community, though, you might see that it
doesn't deliver - across a cohort of people it doesn't
deliver high value.

currently under way within your district that you are aware

example where I have worked previously, just to - would you
like me to give you that?
Q. Yes, please.
A. That I think underscores the difficulty of the issue.
It was in relation to knee arthroscopies for patients over
50 years of age. The health literature is quite clear that
it isn't a procedure that delivers much value in terms of
symptom relief and improvement in function, yet it was
being, across the system, conducted by proceduralists at
quite a high rate. One of the orthopaedic experts and
leaders, Professor Ian Harris, he locked on to this idea
and worked to, I guess, spread the information and talk to
his colleagues about that particular issue, and through
a process of working at that level, the senior clinician
working with colleagues, the system was able to turn that
around, and if you look at the data now as compared to,
say, more than five years, probably 10 years ago, there has
been a demonstrable change in practice.

effected in a model of care that was seen to be low value.

and research, and director of clinical governance, and
I may have missed one.
Q. So that's the means by which the information that
exists within your team is being passed up to that
executive level within the LHD?
A. Yes.
Q. What about the process by which information is
gathered from within your team by you?
A. Yes.
Q. Is there a formal meeting structure?
A. So each of my direct reports has a formal meeting
structure in place for their streams, and then I meet with
my direct reports monthly as well and ask them to report to
me on some specific items.
Q. Is there a standing series of items?
A. Yes.
Q. What are those items?
A. So they cover the kind of range of KPIs that we would
look at, there would be a whole lot of workforce KPIs
around annual leave, vacancies, recruitment, overtime,
budgets as well. There is also the incidents as well, so
if there is any clinical incidents that need to be
reported, they are included in there as well, and mandatory
training for staff is included in those reports as well.
So it kind of tries to mirror as much as possible the
structure that we have to report up to the district and
back to the ministry as well.
Q. So the KPIs that you are looking at in those meetings
are, whilst maybe slightly bespoke for your service,
intended to populate the KPI performance measures for those
same KPIs that are engaged at the district level?
A. Correct.
Q. Which, being the ones which we have spoken of already,
exist in the service agreement?

A. Correct.
Q. In terms of the financial management, do you have
a role in relation to financial management of the mental
health services within the district?
A. So I receive a budget from district finance, so there
is a budget allocation that goes from the service agreement
from ministry to the district and then district finance
allocate a budget out to me as the mental health director.
Q. Can I ask in relation to that, is there a process that
you engage in with the district whereby you work out what
that budget should be?
A. No.
Q. So what is the process in terms of - insofar as you
are aware, at least as the person receiving the budget, how
are decisions made about how big it should be?
A. I receive a budget. So the district gets a budget,
finance looks at activity targets set for community and
inpatient services, then some time after the district has
received their budget from ministry, I get a budget that
comes out to me as mental health director.
Q. So I take it that between the district getting its
budget and you being allocated your budget, there is no
process whereby there is a discussion that happens between
you and, say, finance within the district, about what the
potential needs in terms of mental health care of the
community might be and how much it might cost to deliver?
A. There's been different discussions over the years
about how that process occurs and what the budget setting
mechanism will be.
Q. When you say "different discussions over the years",
how have they differed as the years have rolled on?
A. Sometimes it's been based around FTE targets, around
what is your FTE target for your service. Other times it's
been based around what are your activity targets in terms
of NWAU that has been set for you as a service. Sometimes
it's a combination of both.
Q. So going through them each, the FTE target days, that
was a "This is the number of staff, full time staff
members, that you are going to have, and so here is the
budget that we're going to give you for that"?
A. Yes.

Q. Was there ever a discussion at that point around how
many FTE might have been required to deliver on the mental
health needs of the population within Nepean?
A. Yeah, there was a discussion.
Q. How did it go?
A. It's - I would have liked to have had more - more FTE
allocated.
Q. And in terms of the next discussion or the next form
of assessment that you described, which is the NWAU
discussion, how did that - was there a discussion around
that?
A. No. So they are fixed targets that come - that are
allocated to us.
Q. And is that now the way that it tends to work, as in
has it - is that what happens now or is it --
A. No, it's moved more towards FTEs, more towards
affordable FTE for budget.
Q. So it started with the NWAU, "This is your activity,
this is what you are going to get"?
A. Yep.
Q. It has moved now more to an FTE, "This is how many
people we're going to pay for".
A. Yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. We should understand - "I would
have liked to have had more FTE" in the context you said as
there is a population health need for more FTE?
A. Yes, correct, Commissioner, yes.
MR MUSTON: Q. Whilst workforce challenges you have
spoken about probably mean it's not possible to necessarily
fill every post that you might like to fill, is it your
sense that those workforce challenges are not the limiting
factor but, rather, it's the - well, let me put it another
way. If you were given one more FTE which you felt was
required, do you feel confident that you would be able to
fill it?
A. Yes, for some - but to clarify that answer, for some
professions and areas more than others.
Q. When you say "some", which are the particularly hard

ones to fill?
A. So registered nurse positions in the community are
really difficult to fill, so we have a number of registered
nurse positions within our community mental health teams,
and they are challenging to fill because they don't attract
penalty rates and for registered nurses moving from
inpatient to community teams, they pick up a lot of extra
money through penalty rates from working weekends, working
evenings, working nights, and then to move to a Monday to
Friday community-based team, you lose all of those
penalties, which can have quite a significant financial
impact for those registered nurses.
Q. And that overtime, if they have been engaged in a
community-based setting, is not something that they are
able to pick up in an acute settings?
A. Yes, they do have the option of doing overtime if they
want to do it, but if it's - they do.
Q. Well, what's the challenge? Is it less predictable or
is it less easy for them to facilitate or --
A. It's less predictable. Also the shifts don't always
align, so the community - community teams generally work
8.30 till 5 o'clock. There is kind of a rostering process
that occurs for inpatient units which is different to that.
The community teams are also kind of spread out across the
whole of the district as well, so it might be hard for them
to come and then pick up an overtime shift at Nepean after
they've worked their community shift as well.
Q. So registered nurses in community settings is one of
the challenging spots to fill. Are there others?
A. Yeah, occupational therapists, really hard to fill,
and a number of other allied health professions but
particularly occupational therapists are hard to fill at
the moment in public mental health services.
Q. Is that because there are not many occupational
therapists out there with the experience in the mental
health space, or is it just because they are hard jobs to
fill and there is a lot of other jobs?
A. A lot of them work for NDIS now, so again it's kind
of - there is a much more - within kind of the NDIS space,
there is much higher remuneration available for allied
health people rather than working in the public health
system.

Q. So having been given your budget, how do you go about
monitoring within your - within the mental health service
the extent to which the services you deliver are able to be
brought in within that budget?
A. So we have monthly financial reporting, we have gone
through a process of trying to re-establish a cost centre
by cost centre budget as well, so that we can be really
clear with each cost centre and each cost centre manager
what their budgets and what their targets are for that, and
then we would kind of support them to be able to look at
what aspects of those budgets can they control, can't they
control, what can they change, what can't they influence,
and then we would report that up back to me as an overall
kind of mental health performance.
Q. Each of them presumably is incentivised to deliver the
services they do as efficiently as possible in a financial
sense?
A. I don't - I'm not quite sure what you mean.
Q. So in terms of a budget, a budget is allocated to you?
A. Yes.
Q. You then, cost centre to cost centre --
A. Reallocate that.
Q. -- tally all your reports, this is roughly the amount
that has been allocated to the services you are delivering?
A. Yes.
Q. You encourage them and they no doubt endeavour to
deliver the services that they deliver as efficiently as
possible?
A. Yes. Yes, and try and stay within --
Q. Is it your sense that they do?
A. I think they try really hard to, yeah. They do try to
kind of stay within allocated budget. There is some - some
of the aspects make it more challenging to be able to stay
within it, particularly with the workforce issues we're
having to increasingly use more premium labour,
particularly around medical workforce costs and some
overtime for back-filling nursing agency shifts - not
agencies but back-filling nursing shifts, the use of
premium labour sometimes makes it hard to be able to stay
within budget when you still kind of have to have the same
number of beds open, the same number of getting people

through the emergency departments.
Q. To the extent that things like that increase the costs
of delivering the services that you deliver, do you get
budgetary relief for that from the district?
A. No.
Q. So if it costs you more to deliver a particular
service because you have to rely on premium labour to
a greater extent than had been expected or desired --
A. Yes.
Q. -- the saving to make up for that has to be found
somewhere else within the mental health service; is that
right?
A. Yes.
Q. How do you go about deciding where those savings are
to be made?
A. It's a really hard decision. Sometimes we just kind
of accept that we're going to have to go over budget if
we're going to be able to provide good quality care.
Q. But is it the case that sometimes, services or
particular services within the mental health service do
have to contract in order to accommodate increased costs
like the use of premium labour?
A. Yes.
Q. Are discussions around that and the need to contract
services something which you have with the executive or the
CE within the LHD?
A. Yep. They would either be discussed through my
one-on-one with the CE or they would be raised at the
performance meeting that I have with the district.
Q. So, do you, in your role, have any direct interaction
with the ministry in dealing with the mental health
services that get delivered through Nepean?
A. Well, the - so the meeting that we - we have a really
good relationship with mental health branch, which is one
of the pillars in agency - in ministry, so we have a very
close relationship with mental health branch.
Q. What does that relationship look like? How does it
actually play out? Do you have regular meetings or do
you --

A. Oh, sorry, yes, so the executive director for mental
health is part of mental health branch, so he is our main
kind of conduit into ministry. He chairs the regular
meetings that we have as mental health directors and the
informal meetings that we have as well during that.
There is a number of leads within mental health branch
for specific programs that we are running in mental health
as well, so we have quite close liaison/contact with them
around some specific programs.
Q. So the meetings that you have with the executive
director for mental health of the ministry, what do they -
what sort of topics tend to be discussed at those meetings?
A. So we will generally talk about kind of issues that
are facing the whole mental health system across New South
Wales. We will talk about kind of common pressures that
mental health directors are experiencing and feeling and
we'll talk about if there is significant kind of policy
development or policy work that is being led by ministry.
Q. In terms of the common pressures, are budgetary
pressures one of those items that is regularly discussed at
those meetings?
A. Yes.
Q. And again without inviting you to put words into the
mouths of your colleagues, is the sense that you get that
they share those budgetary pressures?
A. Yes.
Q. We've heard about a mental health program council.
Can you explain what that organisation is?
A. Yes. So it's not an organisation, it's a combination
of the mental health directors and a number of NGOs and
peak bodies that work in the mental health sector, and it
really - it is an evolving meeting, to be honest. So we
just had a meeting last week where we were looking at
reviewing the terms of reference for that meeting. So it
involves BEING, it involves Mental Health Coordinating
Council, it involves the carers' network as well -
apologies, I'm probably getting their titles wrong and they
will be upset with me, but it is a range of different NGOs
and different peak bodies trying to work together, and the
PHNs are involved in it as well.
Q. Do those meetings or the outcome of those meetings

inform in any way the services which you deliver through
the mental health service in Nepean?
A. It's more - quite often it's more of an information
sharing meeting, to be honest. So it is a good opportunity
for us to look at where is there greater areas for
collaboration and integration between the different kind of
players in the mental health field.
Q. When you say collaboration and integration, to the
extent that the NGOs are providing mental health services
within your LHD's footprint --
A. Yes.
Q. -- is part of what you are doing seeking to identify
what they are doing so that you can integrate what you are
doing as best as possible with them and avoid any overlaps?
A. Correct.
Q. Is it a particular challenge within the delivery of
mental health services that there are so many different
organisations that are delivering mental health services
perhaps to the same patient sometimes?
A. Yes.
Q. Yep.
Q. How is the LHD, your LHD, seeking to deal with those
challenges?
A. We're trying to make sure that we coordinate services
around patients and people as much as possible. We have
a really strong view that people needing mental health care
should experience that mental health care as seamless,
regardless as to who is funding it or who is providing it,
that they should experience that care as coordinated and
seamless. So we're trying really hard to make sure that we
have as best relationships and clear points of contact and
escalations through the different NGOs and PHNs that are
working to provide care often to the same person.
Q. What about information sharing about a patient and
their condition?
A. So we need to do that with their consent, and we will
work hard with people to explain the limits of consent,
privacy and confidentiality.
Q. Assuming you have explained it to them and they have
said "Yes, we consent, that would be great if we didn't

have to retell our story every time we came to a different
service", how do you as a service facilitate that sharing
of information that has been consensually shared?
A. There are different ways that we could do it and some
of that would depend on the individual person, the service
being provided and what information is relevant for that
service to be able to make sure that the person is getting
the best care.
Q. Are there any formal structures for that information
sharing that exist between your service, or services, and
the other services delivered by other organisations,
including the NGOs within your LHD?
A. While not specific to individual patients, we do have
a data sharing arrangement with the PHN, which is the
primary health network, and we do have an agreement that we
can share some broad demographic data and particularly
suicide monitoring data and suicide monitoring reports that
we get from ministry - we have a data sharing and
confidentiality agreement that we can share that with the
PHN.
Q. But in terms of a particular patient's experience or
their journey to date through the mental health system,
there is no formal mechanism whereby that information is,
if consent given, shared with anyone else within the system
who might be delivering mental health care to that person?
A. No, I would say there isn't a formal system to do it.
It would probably involve kind of printing out things,
sharing them that way.
Q. So the district presumably reports to the ministry.
Do you have some role in the gathering of information for
the purpose of the district's reporting obligations?
A. Yeah, so the ministry sends out a reporting pack
before we have our meetings with ministry, so we have
regular performance meetings with them. They send out
a performance pack that identifies KPIs that they are
concerned about for each district. We then review those
KPIs when they come out and we submit what strategies we
are putting in place to monitor or improve those KPIs, and
then they get submitted back to ministry, which then become
the meeting papers for the performance meeting.
Q. Do you have any direct engagement with the LHD board?
A. No.

Q. The next thing I would like to ask you about is the
Quadrant report?
A. Yes.
Q. Could you tell us, first of all, what the Quadrant
report is?
A. Yes, so that's a one-page report that we need to
submit to the safe care committee and to the work health
and safety committee. What it does is try to summarise
some of the more detailed reporting that we need to submit
to both of those committees, so that there can be a really
simple kind of highlight of achievements, challenges,
issues that we're working on and issues that need to be
escalated to the committee.
Q. The fact that it is going to those two committees -
would it be right for us to assume that the content of that
Quadrant report is predominantly dealing with patient
safety and workforce safety issues?
A. Yes. Depending on which committee it's going to.
Q. And not descending into detail around an assessment of
the needs of the community and the extent to which they are
able to be met by the services that are being delivered?
A. Correct.
Q. So you said you had no engagement with the board. Do
you - is information passed down to you from the board in
any instance, or are you - is there any way in which the
board is involved in directing or involving itself in the
services that you deliver through your mental health
service?
A. So it comes down through the committees. So if there
is a particular board direction around the KPIs that we're
looking at, that would come back down either through the
meeting I have with the chief executive or back down
through one of the committees that we attend or through the
performance meeting.
Q. Can I ask you some questions about the mental health
strategic plan which, as we understand, is co-developed
with the CCC?
A. Yes.
Q. Just explain what that strategic plan involves --
A. Yes.

Q. -- from your perspective in a practical sense?
A. Yeah, so it really just kind of identifies the key
areas that we really want to try and focus on over
a certain period of time. It isn't directly linked to the
service agreement KPIs that come out through that. It's
more an internally generated strategic plan of wanting to
look at which areas, as an internal mental health service,
we really want to focus on over a period of time.
Q. So how do you go about identifying them?
A. So there was a really big plan - the original plan was
created before I was in the position, and that was created
through a number of workshops and engagements and looking
at some of the bigger strategic plans, I think, that was
done, and we did a refresh of it last year.
Q. And when you did the refresh, what was the refreshment
process?
A. What it was was looking at the actions that were
included within the previous plan, seeing had we actually
made any progress on those actions or whether, if we hadn't
made progress on those actions, trying to understand why
not, and did we want to carry those actions over into the
second half of the strategic plan.
Q. And as part of that process, did you identify actions
which you didn't persevere with?
A. Yeah, we found some actions that we hadn't made
progress on and when we went through a process of saying,
well, do we want to still keep these actions or do we want
to refine the actions that we are really going to target
over the remaining 18 months of the plan - so we ended up
with yes, there were actions under every aim, but we were
really going to focus on probably five actions out of each
aim.
Q. How did you go about identifying what it was that you
wanted to focus on?
A. So we got the whole of the mental health executive
together with the consumer and carer council and we went
through a voting exercise to - I think we had a whole room
covered with white butcher's paper and sticky notes and
things like that and we went through a process of everybody
voting to say, firstly, did we want to keep the action in
the strategic plan; and, secondly, did we then want to
prioritise it for focused action in the remaining time that
we had in that plan.

Q. And to the extent that you have identified those
things to focus on, do you think progress has been made
towards achieving them?
A. Yes.
Q. Can I ask you a little bit more about the consumer and
carer council. How long has it been in operation?
A. So it was formally established in 2019, but there had
been a significant amount of work done into the lead-up of
that about how do we formalise a structure for carer and
consumer engagement within the mental health service.
Consumer and carer engagement has a really long history
within mental health services and a lot of it has been done
kind of either on volunteer bases or ad hoc bases, and we
wanted to make sure that there was a really solid robust
framework around how we would engage with carers and
consumers, and making sure that they had ability to partner
with the mental health service at a high level to make sure
that they were - their voice and their views were heard at
the right level.
Q. In terms of the structure of the council, is it an LHD
specific thing or are you aware of equivalents existing in
other LHDs?
A. So this is just in our mental health service. I know
that most LHDs will have a version of a consumer and carer
council but I don't know the exact specifics of what
other - how other LHDs would run one.
Q. In terms of your consumer and carer council, how many
people sit on it at any given time?
A. Twelve.
Q. How are they chosen?
A. They go through - it is a recruitment, selective
recruitment process. We have six carers and six consumers,
so we have six people who have cared for someone with a
mental illness and then we have six people who've got a
lived experience of a mental illness.
Q. Is there an expression of interest process?
A. Yes.
Q. So it advertises somewhere?
A. We often recruit people who have made complaints or
had poor experiences of care. We will often kind of

actively try and recruit them in to be part of our consumer
and carer council to make sure that we're getting a really
good diverse range of views and that we're not - so it is
a really good diverse range of views within that. We
generally have a waiting list for our council as well. So
we have - when we don't have the waiting list or we have
got vacancies, we have gone out and done more promotion
through the district social media channels as well or other
ways of recruiting people.
Q. Do you find that it is an effective way of engaging
with the consumer and carer population?
A. Absolutely.
Q. To what extent is the feedback - I know we have just
been through the strategic plan but are there any other
ways in which the feedback provided by the council is
directly integrated into or results in changes in the
service that is delivered through your service?
A. Yes, so the council develop their own work plan as
well, so they have a planning day every year, and then they
develop a work plan for the work that they want to do
within the council. I meet with them every time they meet.
I have a half-hour meeting with them as well where they
will present their plan to me, we will have a look at it
and see if that's kind of something that we can kind of
work on and put - whether it is a certain kind of area that
we want to work on together.
Q. Do you have any examples of occasions on which the
outcomes of the council's meetings have resulted in changes
to the services delivered through the mental health
service?
A. Yes, so one of the big ones is what we called our
advance statements, and it's - it was a key project that
the council identified a few years ago, that they really
wanted to come up with a process where people who were
having mental health crises could have what is called an
advance statement, which is very different to anything to
do with voluntary assisted dying or advanced care
directives, but it was really a document that people could
come to either the emergency department or a community
mental health service or any other setting, when they are
in crisis, that really describes how they want to be
supported in a crisis and how they don't want to be
supported in a crisis. So one of the things we've learned
from the CCC really strongly was that asking people to

retell their story, asking people to do lots of kind of
tricky questions when they are in a crisis is probably the
worst time to be doing it, so they went through a co-design
approach of developing a document where it could be filled
in when people aren't in crisis so that they could then
present this and have that as a guide for how they want to
be supported when they are in crisis.
Q. Now, do you have any particular arrangements,
strategies or programs which are in place for the delivery
of mental health care to First Nations people within your
LHD?
A. So over the last 12 months we have just stood up an
Indigenous advisory council, which very much mirrors the
structure of the consumer and carer council, in that it
would again be recruited to in the same way and it would
sit on the same level of the organisational chart and it
would work specifically in the same way as the consumer and
carer council has worked to support me and my executive,
but it would have a specific Indigenous and First Nations
approach.
Q. So it is - has it stood up yet, or is it being stood
up?
A. They've had two meetings, two or three meetings.
Q. And have you - so early days. But have you found
that - have you received any output from those meetings or
from that --
A. They are still working their way through how they want
to work, and I don't want - I want them to find their own
way through how they want to work. So they are still going
through a process of how - what do they want to be called,
how do they want to invite people to be part of it, how do
they want to work with me and work with the service, so I'm
giving them time to do that.
Q. What is it that you are hoping, if it works as well as
it can, to achieve through the standing up of this
committee? What input into the way in which services are
delivered are they going to provide, do you hope?
A. What I'm hoping is - what we have found with the CCC
is that it really gave us a kind of bottom-up approach to
what we needed to be doing better, and the CCC had really
good engagement with consumers and carers at lots of
levels, which wasn't someone officially from the service
meeting with them. We would get a lot of kind of anecdotal

feedback coming up through the committee, but also it would
give them the opportunity, like, to kind of really say,
"You've got to focus a bit more on this area. You've got
to do a bit more around this." We're hoping that the
Indigenous council has the same thing in that it's
actually, as it is Indigenous led and chaired by our
Aboriginal Indigenous workers, that it will be a much safer
place and a cultural place for people to raise concerns.
Q. When you mentioned a minute ago the need to focus more
on a particular area, is that particular areas within
services that are being delivered, in the sense that you
need to adjust in a slight way the way in which services
are delivered, or is it - are you talking about focusing on
a particular area being an unmet area of mental health need
within the community?
A. Yeah, I think there's so much unmet mental health need
across the community everywhere. For these two bodies,
they are generally focused more on things we can do better
within our existing services.
Q. You have mentioned the Primary Health Network. Do you
have any formal engagement with the Primary Health Network
other than through the meetings that you referred to
a minute ago, which were the mental health program council
meetings?
A. So we have a - there is a board subcommittee that we -
that I co-chair with my equivalent over in the Primary
Health Network, which is the Joint Regional Mental Health
Suicide Prevention Plan Committee. We have to have a joint
regional mental health and suicide prevention plan which is
between our services and the PHN. We have a committee that
oversees the operationalisation of that plan and the
delivery of that plan. That's our formal structure around
how do we work with the PHN.
Q. So is the formal structure built around programs
delivered through or facilitated through the PHN which are
funded in part or whole by the Commonwealth?
A. It's a bit of both. So there are some programs which
are jointly funded through state funding and Commonwealth
funding under the new bilateral agreements, so we oversee
some of those programs. It's also a broader plan that
looks at how do we work with people like Lifeline, how do
we work with non-PHN funded or non-health funded services
to again try and make sure that we're providing joined up
and integrated care for people in our district.

Q. Insofar as you are aware, does the PHN have a pool of
discretionary funds that it and you can collaborate to work
out how best to spend?
A. Yes, yes.
Q. How does that process work in terms of deciding how
you should collaborate to spend pooled resources?
A. Yeah, we generally kind of have a conversation between
me and my equivalent at the PHN, and they will say "We've
got a bit of money left over, we've got some discretionary
funding. Where do you think it would be best placed, what
do you think would be the best way of using it?" We will
link it back to - if there is something from the joint
regional plan that we can think, "Well, this needs a bit of
funding, let's have a look at that", or if there is just
kind of feedback that we're hearing from the clinical teams
or clinicians around gaps in terms of what is being offered
for people at the moment.
Q. In terms of the funding, the PHN funding which is tied
to particular programs, do you have a view about whether
those programs - let's start in the general - are usually
or always the best way of spending the resources that have
been deployed toward them, or is it your view, sometimes,
that the programs are not necessarily the best way of
spending money which has been earmarked for mental health?
Maybe it would be easier if I asked you to sort of run
through the programs. Pick a few of them.
A. So the programs that they kind of fund are the Head to
Health centres. I think that that's a really good use of
Commonwealth funding. I think what we're trying to look at
is how to manage that difference between what's kind of
primary health interventions, which are generally
Commonwealth and PHN funded, and then what is the kind of
more specialist or tertiary interventions which come
